description: Chemical Engineering student from Nicaragua who builds tech solutions: Python, JavaScript, React Native, Django, IoT and data analysis. I’ve worked in sugar mill quality control and like turning engineering problems into simple, validated tools for agroindustry and sustainability. Join us to turn NASA data into a tool for Nicaraguan farmers. Looking for: agronomy/agricultural engineering, GIS and remote sensing, UX/UI design, statistics, and strong presentation skills.
summary: We developed Canícula, a web decision-support tool that helps farmers in Nicaragua compare crop-rotation strategies using NASA Earth observation data. For any selected coordinate, the system retrieves eight core variables in real time, without storing large files: precipitation, surface and root-zone soil moisture, solar radiation and temperature (NASA POWER); slope and terrain convergence from global elevation models (SRTM-based Terrain Tiles and Copernicus DEM); and soil texture and organic carbon (ISRIC SoilGrids). From these we compute FAO-56 evapotranspiration, water and heat stress yield penalties (FAO-33), RUSLE erodibility and available water capacity. Each rotation strategy, including the current one, is scored and explained: why it is suggested, the supporting evidence, expected benefits, information gaps and risks requiring local expert review. The tool addresses the challenge by turning long-term satellite and terrain data into clear, farmer-friendly comparisons of water use, erosion and soil health, accounting for the mid-summer drought (canícula). It matters because smallholders in dry regions face unpredictable rainfall and soil degradation and need accessible evidence that supports, not replaces, local agronomic judgment.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Canícula is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers in Nicaragua compare crop-rotation strategies. The user selects a coordinate, and the system retrieves in real time eight core environmental, topographic, and soil variables: daily precipitation, surface and root-zone soil moisture, solar radiation, and temperatures (NASA POWER); terrain slope and convergence derived from global elevation models (Mapzen Terrain Tiles, which incorporate SRTM, and the Copernicus DEM via Open-Meteo); and soil texture and organic carbon (ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0). [Additional NASA Earth observation products (GPM IMERG precipitation, SMAP soil moisture, and Landsat and MODIS vegetation indices) support the analysis of rainfall, soil moisture, and exposed-soil periods.]

From these data we compute reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56), yield penalties from water and heat stress (FAO-33), soil erodibility (RUSLE K-factor), and available water capacity. Each rotation strategy, including the farmer’s current one, is evaluated against these indicators and explained: why it is suggested, what evidence supports it, what benefits it may offer, where information gaps exist, and which risks need local expert review.

Benefits and expected impact

The tool gives farmers information they rarely have today: how rainfall and soil moisture have changed, when fields are exposed to erosion, and how the mid-summer drought (canícula) affects each crop. We expect it to help reduce soil loss, use water more efficiently, and diversify with lower risk, especially in dry regions such as Nicaragua’s Dry Corridor. It is designed to support, not replace, farmer judgment and local agronomic expertise.

Tools and technologies used

Programming languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML [and CSS, plus any frameworks or libraries]. Data sources: NASA POWER, [GPM IMERG, SMAP, MERRA-2, Landsat, MODIS,] SRTM (via Mapzen Terrain Tiles on AWS), Copernicus DEM GLO-90 (via Open-Meteo), and ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0. Methods: FAO-56, FAO-33, RUSLE, and pedotransfer functions to classify soils under the USDA system. Hardware: none.

What makes it creative?

  • It integrates climate, terrain, and soil into a single evaluation per rotation strategy, instead of showing separate maps.
  • Scoring is explainable: the tool shows the problems detected for the selected location and which criteria drove each recommendation, so users can see why a strategy is suggested.
  • It accounts for the mid-summer drought (canícula) and periods of exposed soil, the moments of greatest vulnerability in Nicaraguan farming systems.
  • It queries data in real time instead of storing large files, which reduces resource use and keeps the web application lightweight.

Factors our team considered

  • Limited connectivity in rural areas: the web application is lightweight and requests only the data needed for the selected location, which keeps data usage low on slow connections.
  • Users without technical training: plain language and comparable results.
  • Data resolution: climate analysis is zonal, not parcel-level. It gives a regional picture of the conditions that affect crops, while terrain and soil layers add finer-scale detail. We state this limit openly.
  • Modeled soil data: SoilGrids is an estimate and requires field validation.
  • Local validation: agronomic rules and recommendations must be reviewed by local specialists.
  • National sources: we consider INETER, for meteorological, climatic, and geographic information, and the Universidad Nacional Agraria (UNA), for research on soils, agricultural production, and sustainable management, as reference sources that can complement the analysis and help adapt recommendations to the conditions of Nicaragua’s Dry Corridor.
